title: Following authors and checking their new releases
tagline: Follow the authors you like and see from your own shelf when they have a new book out
overview:
- Add the AuthorFollow table and domain model, capped at 50 authors per user ＝ the writers you read most become a watchlist that lives with your shelf
- Teach the Rakuten Books search to query by author, newest release first, and keep the release date ＝ that author's books line up newest first with their dates, so an unread one is obvious at a glance
- Add four GraphQL operations — followedAuthors / authorNewReleases / followAuthor / unfollowAuthor ＝ the screen and the server now agree on how this data moves, so a phone app or a notification can reuse the same path later
- Add the `/authors` page and a follow button next to the author name on a book ＝ you can follow straight from the book you just finished, and see every new release on one page
- Only the owner can see or change their own follows ＝ nobody else can tell which authors you are following

groups.title: The data model for following an author
groups.intent: Lay the groundwork for storing who follows which author. The table (Prisma), the domain model that owns the rules, the persistence interface and its Prisma implementation all land together as one set.
groups.impact: Includes a DB schema change: the users table gains a relation, and the schema is defined in two places — apps/api and apps/web — because both apps talk to the same database.

sections.title: The author_follows table
sections.explain: A table holding a user ID and an author name (up to 120 characters). A unique constraint on (userId, authorName) means the same author cannot be registered twice. Deleting a user deletes their follows with it (onDelete: Cascade). The same definition goes into the schema.prisma of both apps/api and apps/web.

sections.title: The AuthorFollow domain model
sections.explain: The rules for an author name are sealed inside the model. Surrounding whitespace is trimmed, and neither an empty string nor `-` is accepted as a name (kidoku stores `-` as the author of a book whose author is unknown). The 120-character limit lives here too. The constructor is private, so there are only two ways in: create for a new follow and fromDatabase for one restored from the DB — id is null on create and present on restore.

annotations.text: A book with an unknown author is stored with `-` as its author name, so it is rejected the same way an empty string is.
Only two ways to build one — create (new) and fromDatabase (restore) — so an instance that skipped validation cannot exist.

sections.title: Persistence interface and its Prisma implementation
sections.explain: Use cases depend only on the abstract class IAuthorFollowRepository; the Prisma-backed implementation sits in infrastructure and is swapped in by NestJS DI. The list comes back oldest first, and deletion keys on both id and userId. Prisma rows are never returned as they are — toEntity turns them into the domain model.

groups.title: Author search and release dates from the Rakuten Books API
groups.intent: The new-release check needs the book search to be callable as "by author, newest release first". Everything the title search and the author search share — reading credentials, building parameters, shaping the response — moves into a private search(), and only the differing parts are passed in.
groups.impact: Runs through the same code as the existing title search (used when registering a book). The way parameters are assembled changed, so that existing search is in the blast radius.

sections.title: Extending the search interface
sections.explain: BookSearchItem gains an optional release date (salesDate) and IBookSearchRepository gains searchByAuthor. The release date is optional on purpose: only the author search fills it in.

sections.title: Extracting the shared search()
sections.explain: The API call searchByTitle used to own moves into a private search(), leaving the caller to decide the search conditions. Title search keeps its 30 hits; author search asks for 10, newest release first (sort: -releaseDate). The response mapping now keeps salesDate, so the screen can show a release date.

annotations.text: Ten hits, newest release first — a new book shows up at the top.
outOfStockFlag stays a shared parameter, so the author search includes out-of-stock books. Worth confirming that is intended for a new-release check.

groups.title: Use cases for the follow operations
groups.intent: Follow, unfollow, list and new-releases become four use cases, one responsibility each. The decisions that belong to the application — the cap, what a duplicate means — are collected here.
groups.impact: Additions only; no existing use case was touched.

sections.title: Following and unfollowing
sections.explain: Following an author who is already followed returns the existing record, so pressing the button twice is not an error. Otherwise the current count is checked and the call fails once 50 authors are reached. Unfollowing first confirms the follow really belongs to the caller by looking it up in their own list, and throws NotFoundException when it does not — someone else's follow ID cannot be deleted. The tests cover three cases: a successful follow, an already-followed author, and going over the cap.

annotations.text: Already following? Return the existing record. Pressing the button twice is not an error.
The per-user cap. Going over it produces the error message the screen shows verbatim.
Checks the follow belongs to the caller before deleting. Passing someone else's follow ID gets a NotFound.

sections.title: Reading the list and the new releases
sections.explain: The list is a thin pass-through to the repository. New-releases trims the author name and returns an empty array without calling the external API when it is blank, which keeps pointless Rakuten API calls out.

groups.title: Exposing it as a GraphQL API
groups.intent: Make the use cases reachable from the screen: input/output types (DTOs), a resolver and the dependency wiring (Module), then register it in the app itself.
groups.impact: Adds 2 queries and 2 mutations to the GraphQL schema, plus one registration in app.module.ts.

sections.title: Input and output types
sections.explain: Inputs for follow, unfollow and new-releases; outputs for a follow and for a new release. Domain models are never handed out directly — they are repacked into this layer's types first. Only the release date is nullable, because Rakuten does not always have one.

sections.title: The resolver
sections.explain: Four operations: followedAuthors (the caller's own follows), authorNewReleases (a given author's new books), followAuthor and unfollowAuthor. The whole resolver sits behind GqlAuthGuard, and the user ID comes from @CurrentUser — a userId sent by the client is never used.

annotations.text: The whole resolver requires authentication. The user ID comes from @CurrentUser, never from a value sent by the client.

sections.title: Dependency wiring and registration
sections.explain: The Module lists the use cases as providers and binds the abstract classes IAuthorFollowRepository / IBookSearchRepository to their implementations — those two entries are why the use cases never need to know about Prisma or the Rakuten API. Finally app.module.ts adds AuthorFollowModule to its imports.

groups.title: The page for followed authors and their new releases
groups.intent: Put adding, removing and checking new releases on one page. The GraphQL definitions live in features/author-follow/api and are imported by the components.
groups.impact: Adds the new /authors page, which redirects to the top page when nobody is signed in.

sections.title: GraphQL query definitions
sections.explain: The queries and mutations matching the four server operations, plus the types the screen uses, all collected in one place. Components only import them.

sections.title: The author-follow page
sections.explain: Type an author name to follow them, and the registered authors line up as tags. Pressing a tag selects that author, and only the selected author's new releases are fetched — with nothing selected the query is skipped. Pressing again deselects. Unfollowing asks for confirmation first and clears the selection if the removed author was the selected one. Server-side error messages, such as the 50-author cap, are shown verbatim in red. The page itself checks the session during SSR and sends anyone signed out back to the top.

sections.title: The follow toggle button
sections.explain: It fetches the follow list and switches its label and action depending on whether this author is in it — "Following" unfollows, otherwise it follows. For a book whose author is blank or `-` the button is not rendered at all. After each action the list is refetched so the display matches.

groups.title: Ways in from the existing screens
groups.intent: A new page nobody can find is a new page nobody uses, so add two entry points: the book detail (next to the author name) and the settings page.
groups.impact: A few added lines in existing components.

sections.title: A button next to the author name on a book
sections.explain: The follow button sits beside the author name in the read-book modal. It only appears on your own shelf (isMine), so it never shows up while you are looking at someone else's.

annotations.text: The button only appears on your own shelf; it is not rendered on someone else's.
